title: SimBench: Can LLMs Really Think Like People?
one_liner: A large-scale benchmark reveals that instruction-tuning helps LLMs agree with consensus but makes them worse at capturing human disagreement.
lead: Large language models are being used to simulate how humans think and decide. But do they actually behave like humans, or just like a smoothed-out majority? SimBench is a unified test covering 20 real human behavior datasets, showing that the best LLMs today capture human choices only 40 percent of the time, and revealing a surprising trap: when you train an LLM to be aligned (safe and helpful), you often make it worse at simulating the full range of actual human opinions.

problem.h2: LLMs as human-behavior simulators are untested and fragmented
paras: Researchers want to use large language models to predict how humans will decide, vote, consume, or answer moral questions. It sounds plausible: if you ask an LLM a question a million humans answered, can it guess the pattern of answers (what fraction said yes, what fraction said no, etc.)? But right now, every researcher uses a different test, different metrics, different datasets. One lab tests moral reasoning on 100 people, another tests economic choices on 50. There is no common ruler to say when or why an LLM really succeeds at simulating humans.

A beginner might try: just ask the LLM the question, count what it says, and compare to what humans said. That almost works. But it fails in two critical ways. First, models trained to be aligned (safe and helpful) are steered toward what most people believe, not toward the full range of human opinion. Second, a model's training data already contains millions of human opinions, so it is hard to know whether it is simulating humans or just repeating its training set.

callout.html: There is no standardized way to measure when LLMs faithfully capture how humans actually think, including the many cases where humans disagree.

panels.title: 1. The dream

panels.title: 3. The aligned trap

panels.caption: Alignment steers the model toward the majority. On consensus questions (95% agree), that helps. On divided questions (50-50), it fails.

panels.title: 5. The trap springs

steps.text: Collect real human responses to moral, economic, and behavioral questions from thousands of people across multiple countries.
For each question, ask the model to assign a probability to each answer (yes / no / agree / disagree / etc.), matching what a human does.
Compute a score: how close is the model's guess of the human response pattern to the actual human response pattern? Lower is worse.
Separate questions by human-answer diversity: consensus (95% agree on one answer) vs. pluralistic (people split 50-50). Score each.

For the same model, measure performance before and after instruction-tuning. Tuning helps on consensus questions (humans agree) but hurts on disagreement questions (humans split), because alignment narrows the model's outputs toward a single answer.

paras: SimBench measures something most existing benchmarks ignore: the model's internal confidence distribution over answer choices. Instead of just asking did the model pick the right answer (yes/no), it asks: does the model believe answers in the same proportions humans do? For consensus questions (95% of humans say yes), the model should output 95%. For contested questions (50% yes, 50% no), the model should output 50-50%. A normal test gets both right only by accident. SimBench forces the model to show its actual belief distribution and grades it on fidelity.
object.object: how a model distributes confidence across multiple answer choices

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: how alignment erases disagreement
hidden.name: disagreement score (how much the aligned model's answer pattern differs from human disagreement)
paras: When humans answer a question, some questions show high agreement (everyone says yes), and some show high disagreement (half say yes, half say no). Aligned models systematically narrow their answer choices: they converge toward the majority opinion, flattening disagreement. This paper measures that shift and discovers it is the core trade-off: alignment kills simulation of human disagreement.

The paper computes this by measuring how much humans split on each question, then measuring how much an aligned model narrows that split compared to a base model. On questions where humans disagree sharply, the aligned model's answers narrow sharply downward toward a fake majority. That is the alignment-simulation tradeoff.

cells: Aligned narrows toward the human consensus
Aligned moves from 52-48 to 70-30, farther from actual 50-50
heat.caption: Darker means better match to human response distribution. On consensus (high darkness, left), aligned models match humans. On disagreement (low darkness, right), aligned models diverge from humans.

reads.html: When humans are divided on a question (50% say yes, 50% say no), alignment training steers the model toward a fake majority (70% yes, 30% no), so it misses the real human split.

The pre-training objective of a base model tries to match the full spread of human opinions: if humans split 50-50, the model learns to output 50-50. Post-training (instruction tuning) retrains the model to pick one answer as best, narrowing its outputs toward a single majority view. This works when humans actually agree (the consensus really is the right answer), but fails when humans disagree (the model's narrowed answer misses the real split).

paras: A base language model is trained on billions of sentences from the internet. Its training goal is simple: predict the next word. This goal naturally leads the model to learn the full range of human opinion in its training data. When asked a controversial question, the base model outputs probabilities that reflect the real human split. If humans are 50-50, the model learns to output 50-50.

But then, for safety and helpfulness, researchers apply instruction-tuning: they show the model examples of aligned (safe, helpful, consensus) answers and steer it toward those. This changes the model's internal goal. Now the model is trained to converge toward whatever the trainers marked as the right answer. On easy consensus questions (nearly everyone agrees), this is great: the model aligns with human consensus and gets better, because the consensus answer really is what most humans think. But on contested questions (people genuinely disagree), this training objective works against simulation. The aligned model has been steered toward a false majority, so when asked a controversial moral question, it gives a single confident answer instead of capturing the actual human disagreement. The base model, not yet pushed toward consensus, still reflects the real distribution.

stages.s: A moral or economic question with diverse human responses
Base model: learns mass-covering goal (match full range of human opinions)
Output: probability distribution matching human split, even on divided questions
Aligned model: trained to converge toward consensus answers
Output: confidence narrowed toward majority, even when humans disagree
On split questions, aligned model diverges from human distribution

math.words: For each question i, compute the squared difference between the model's predicted answer probability and the human answer probability, then normalize against the baseline.
math.equation: S_i = Σ_k [human_prob(answer_k) - model_prob(answer_k)]^2, normalized by dataset mean baseline
symbols: simulation score for question i (lower is worse; perfect match is 0)
fraction of humans who gave answer k (e.g. 0.50 for half the sample)
model's predicted probability for answer k
average score for all questions to ensure numerical stability

worked.title: A worked example: one question
lines: Question: Do you support policy X? Humans: 60% yes, 40% no.
Aligned model's error is 56x higher on this one question. Across all diverse questions, aligned models accumulate much higher error than base models.

math.note: The smaller the squared difference between what the model predicts and what humans actually said, the better the simulator, because the model is placing its confidence mass (its probabilities) in the same places humans do.

bars.h2: Simulation ability by model size and training stage

charts.title: Best LLMs today (size effect)
charts.note: Performance scales log-linearly with model size: doubling the model size gives a small, steady gain. The best LLMs score around 40-41 out of 100, still far from human fidelity.

charts.title: Base vs. Aligned (the tradeoff)
charts.note: On consensus, alignment lifts performance by 6 points. On diverse questions, alignment crashes it by 12 points. The tradeoff is real and large.

items.html: The model may have seen some of these datasets during training. However, SimBench uses zero-shot aggregation (asking for a distribution, not reciting specific examples), which largely mitigates this risk.

Asking an aligned model directly for a distribution is different from asking a base model. Aligned models may verbalize their answer differently than base models show in their internal probabilities. The paper tests that the method works consistently, but measurement bias persists.

items.b: Letting models think longer does not rescue the tradeoff.
items.html: The paper tested whether letting models take more computational steps (like chain-of-thought reasoning) could overcome the alignment-simulation gap. It did not. The gap is fundamental, not a reasoning depth issue, because the problem is the aligned model's training objective itself, not its reasoning ability.

The benchmark covers diverse questions, but the participant pool is still skewed toward Anglophone Western respondents. Models fail harder on questions involving traits that conflict with alignment objectives, which often means they fail on the beliefs of minority groups.

items.b: Done right: use base models for social simulation.
items.html: If you want an LLM to capture human disagreement, do not use an aligned model. Use the base model before post-training, even if it is less safe. Or re-align after simulation, at the cost of a small degradation, because the base model's spread-out answers are closer to human reality.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small test with two questions: one where humans strongly agree (e.g., 95% of humans think jumping off a cliff is bad), and one where humans are split (e.g., 50% prefer coffee, 50% prefer tea). Collect predictions from a base LLM and an aligned LLM (e.g., Llama-2-base vs. Llama-2-chat). For each model and question, sample 100 times and compute the distribution. Then compute how far each model's distribution is from the true human distribution. You should see: on the consensus question, aligned wins; on the split question, base wins by a large margin.
demo.metric_eq: divergence = Σ |model_prob(k) - human_prob(k)| for all answer options k
demo.closing: The single fact a demo must make impossible to miss: alignment training narrows a model's output distribution (pushing it toward one answer), which helps on consensus questions (because the consensus really is what most humans think) but actively harms on disagreement questions (because humans truly are split, and the aligned model gives a false majority).
